An abstract polymer model consists of an at most countable set $\Gamma$ (finite or in bijection with $\mathbb N$), a reflexive symmetric relation $\sim$ on $\Gamma$ (so $\gamma\sim\gamma$ and $\gamma\sim\eta$ implies $\eta\sim\gamma$), and an activity function $z:\Gamma\to\mathbb C$. Its elements are called polymers, and $\gamma\sim\eta$ means that the two polymers are incompatible. A subset $X\subseteq\Gamma$ is compatible when no two distinct elements of $X$ are related by $\sim$. For real and natural summands, finite-index sums and products are enumeration-independent. For complex summands, define a finite sum or product by any enumeration and repeated addition or multiplication in $\mathbb C$; associativity and commutativity make the result independent of the enumeration. The empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. For each finite $V\subseteq\Gamma$, define the finite-volume partition polynomial

$$Z_V(z):=\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq V\\X\text{ compatible}}}\ \prod_{\gamma\in X}z_\gamma,$$

where the empty subset contributes $1$.

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $\binom{[n]}2:=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i\ne j\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is a pair $([n],E)$ with $E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and each consecutive pair an edge. A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path. A cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and each consecutive pair an edge; a tree is a connected simple graph with no cycle. For $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the set of connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the set of trees on $[n]$. The set $[n]$ is finite; its power set is finite, so its subset $\binom{[n]}2$ is finite; the power set of that edge set is finite as well. Each simple graph on $[n]$ is determined by an edge set in this last power set, so $\mathcal C_n$ and $\mathcal T_n$ are finite.

For an ordered tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\Gamma^n$, put $f_{ij}:=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$ and define the connected coefficient

$$U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}.$$

For $n=1$, $\mathcal C_1$ contains the one-vertex graph and the empty edge product equals $1$. These are finite polynomial and coefficient definitions; they assert no convergence.

A **finite simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a finite
set and

$$E\subseteq [V]^2:=\{\,\{u,v\}\subseteq V: u\ne v\,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus every edge has two distinct endpoints, there are no loops,
and an unordered pair of vertices occurs as at most one edge. Finiteness and the
notation $|V|$ and $|E|$ are those of [[def-finite-cardinality]].

When no qualifier is present, the word **graph** has this meaning.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply The recursion theorem with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line (Every subset of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, agreeing with the real supremum and infimum on nonempty sets bounded in $\mathbb{R}$). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $G$ be a graph. A **spanning tree** of $G$ is a spanning subgraph $T$ of $G$ that is a tree ([[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]], [[def-tree-forest-and-leaf]]). Equivalently,

$$V(T)=V(G),\qquad E(T)\subseteq E(G),$$

and $T$ is connected and acyclic.

The null graph has no spanning tree under the library convention that a tree is nonempty and connected.
A finite graph $G$ is connected if and only if it has a spanning tree.
Every finite graph has only finitely many spanning trees.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $F$ be a field (Field) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann), The recursion theorem):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

A tree has a unique path between any two vertices: connectedness gives a path, and two distinct paths would contain a cycle between their first divergence and next common vertex, contradicting acyclicity. Here is the cut and exchange argument used below. Let $f=\{u,v\}$ be an edge of a tree $T$. There is no $u$-$v$ path in $T-f$, since such a path together with $f$ would be a cycle in $T$. $$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so

A **simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a set and

$$E \subseteq [V]^2 := \{\, \{u,v\} \subseteq V : u \ne v \,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus a simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges.

This is the same incidence convention as [[def-finite-simple-graph]], with the
word "finite" removed from the hypothesis on $V$. Whenever a statement on this
page is made for a simple graph, it allows an arbitrary vertex set unless
finiteness is stated separately.

A **finite simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a finite
set and

$$E\subseteq [V]^2:=\{\,\{u,v\}\subseteq V: u\ne v\,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus every edge has two distinct endpoints, there are no loops,
and an unordered pair of vertices occurs as at most one edge. Finiteness and the
notation $|V|$ and $|E|$ are those of [[def-finite-cardinality]].

When no qualifier is present, the word **graph** has this meaning.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph in the sense of
[[def-simple-graph-without-a-finiteness-hypothesis]].

A **walk**, **closed walk**, **trail**, **path**, and **cycle** in $G$ are
defined exactly as in [[def-graph-walk-trail-path-and-cycle]], with no
finiteness hypothesis on $V$. In particular, a walk is a finite vertex list
$$(v_0,\dots,v_\ell)$$
with $\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\in E$ for each $1 \le i \le \ell$, and a path is a walk
with distinct vertices.

Vertices $u,v \in V$ are **connected** when some path in $G$ has endpoints $u$
and $v$. The graph $G$ is **connected** when $V \ne \emptyset$ and every two
vertices of $G$ are connected.

For $v \in V$, the **connected component** of $v$ is the induced subgraph on
$$C_G(v) := \{\, u \in V : u \text{ is connected to } v \,\}.$$

These are the same notions as in [[def-connected-graph-and-connected-component]],
again with the finiteness hypothesis removed.

Let $G$ be a simple graph.

A **cycle** in $G$ is a cycle in the sense of
[[def-graph-walk-trail-path-and-cycle]], that is, a closed walk of length at
least $3$ whose vertices are distinct except for the repeated endpoint.

The graph $G$ is **acyclic** if it contains no cycle.

A **tree** is a connected acyclic simple graph.

A **forest** is an acyclic simple graph.

Let $G$ be a graph. A **spanning tree** of $G$ is a spanning subgraph $T$ of $G$ that is a tree ([[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]], [[def-tree-forest-and-leaf]]). Equivalently,

$$V(T)=V(G),\qquad E(T)\subseteq E(G),$$

and $T$ is connected and acyclic.

The null graph has no spanning tree under the library convention that a tree is nonempty and connected.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $A$ be a finite set and $n := \lvert A\rvert$. Then the power set
$\mathcal{P}(A)$ is finite and

$$\lvert\mathcal{P}(A)\rvert = 2^{\,n},$$

the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].
Moreover $n < 2^{\,n}$.

The last inequality is the quantitative form, for finite $A$, of Cantor's
theorem $A \prec \mathcal{P}(A)$ ([[thm-cantor-powerset]]), which holds for every
set whatsoever. The two statements are consistent and the proof below derives the
inequality from Cantor's theorem rather than leaving them side by side.

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection
   $f : A \to A$ is a bijection.

Clause 3 is the finite form of the Dedekind statement: a finite set is not
equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

If $U_I=+\infty$, the adopted convention gives $e^{-2\beta U_I}=0$; otherwise all pair values in the sum are finite. In either case the exponential definition and addition law [F2], together with evenness of $v$, give $\prod_{i\in I}\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|=e^{-2\beta U_I}$. Stability and monotonicity [F1, F2] imply this product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$. Writing $q_i=\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|$, all $q_i$ are nonnegative and their product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$; hence some $r\in I$ has $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$.

The maps $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto x_i-x_j$ are continuous and hence Borel under [A1, F4]. Since $v$ is Borel [F1], composition with $v$ is Borel [F4]. The adopted map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is Borel: on $\mathbb R$ it is continuous by [F2], and its value at the Borel singleton $+\infty$ is $0$ by [F4]. Thus $f_\beta$ is Borel, and $U_n$ is a finite sum of finite products of Borel factors [F4]. The same composition and arithmetic facts on $\mathbb R^{dn}$ make each tree weight Borel. Its component cannot contain another vertex of $I$, and the set $K\subseteq J$ of its neighbors gives exactly the roots of the resulting branches; this is a bijection with forests in $\mathcal F_{I'\cup K}(J\setminus K)$. The exponential addition law [F2] factors the size weight, so $h(I,J)=e^{2\beta B}\sum_{K\subseteq J}(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)h(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)$. If $I=\varnothing$, both $g$ and $h$ are $1$ for $J=\varnothing$ and $0$ otherwise. Induct on $|I|+|J|$ from these base cases. Step 1.1 supplies the root bound and step 2.1 supplies the graph recurrence; applying the finite-sum real triangle inequality from [F12, F13] gives $|g(I,J)|\leq q_r\sum_K(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)|g(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)|$. The induction hypothesis and $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$ bound this by $h(I,J)$. At $I=\{1\}$, $J=\{2,\ldots,n\}$, $g(I,J)=U_n$ and every forest in $\mathcal F_I(J)$ is a spanning tree. This proves the pointwise tree bound.

In the Prüfer encoding, repeatedly delete the least-labelled leaf and record its neighbor; after $n-2$ deletions this gives a word of length $n-2$ over $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Step 2.2 guarantees a leaf other than the root at every stage with at least two vertices, and deleting a leaf leaves a tree until the final vertex pair. At each stage a vertex occurs in the remaining word exactly once for each incident edge deleted before that vertex; it is recorded when a neighboring leaf is removed, and the vertex itself is deleted once it becomes a leaf, except for the final two vertices. Thus its occurrence count is its current degree minus one, and absence from the word is equivalent to being a current leaf. Conversely, from any such word, repeatedly join the least label absent from the remaining word to its first symbol and delete that label and symbol, then join the last two labels. Adding a new vertex with one edge to a tree makes the new vertex a leaf and preserves connectedness and acyclicity; induction on the word length therefore shows this constructs a tree. In the resulting tree the least absent label is a leaf and the first symbol is its neighbor, so encoding reverses every decoding step. The procedures give a bijection with all $n^{n-2}$ words. Integrating the pointwise tree bound of step 3.1 and using monotonicity, homogeneity and finite additivity [F8, F9] with the tree integral from step 2.2 yields $\int|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq2$ and write $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is $([n],E)$ with $E$ a set of unordered two-element subsets of $[n]$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and consecutive pairs in $E$; connected means every two vertices are joined by a path; a cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and consecutive pairs in $E$; a tree is a connected graph with no cycle; a forest is a graph with no cycle. Finite sums and products over graph, edge, vertex, and subset sets below are enumeration-independent; the empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. Fix $d\in\mathbb N$ with $d\geq1$, let $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be an even Borel pair potential with no $-\infty$ values, and suppose it is stable with constant $B\in\mathbb R$, $B\geq0$. Fix $\beta\in\mathbb R$ with $\beta>0$, set $e^{-c(+\infty)}:=0$ for every $c>0$, define the Mayer function $f_\beta(x):=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and suppose

$$C_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty.$$

Let $\mathcal C_n$ be the connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the trees on $[n]$. These families are finite because $[n]$ has finitely many unordered two-element subsets and each graph is determined by a subset of those edges. A spanning tree of a finite graph is a tree with the same vertex set and a subset of its edges. A leaf is a vertex incident to exactly one edge. Put

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j).$$

For every configuration $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in(\mathbb R^d)^n$,

$$|U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}|f_\beta(x_i-x_j)|,$$

where $\mathcal T_n$ is the set of labelled trees on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. In particular,

$$\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{\,n-1}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

derivations.claim: For every $N$-point configuration, the energy $E_N=\sum_{i<j}v(x_i-x_j)$ is an extended-real Borel function: coordinate differences are continuous and hence Borel [F13], composition with $v$ preserves Borel measurability [F11], and finite sums preserve it wherever defined. The map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on the extended real line, assigned $0$ at $+\infty$ and $+\infty$ at $-\infty$, is Borel because it is continuous on $\mathbb R$ [F12] and the endpoints are Borel [F14]. Thus the Boltzmann integrand is Borel on $\mathbb R^{dN}$. For $N\geq2$, repeated application of the two-factor product identity [F15] identifies the finite product Borel sigma-algebra; the Borel-to-Lebesgue inclusion [F16] then makes the integrand product-measurable. For $N=0$ or $1$ the same measurability is immediate from the empty or one-factor product. The same extended exponential map and the Borel potential show that $f_\beta$ is Borel. Stability [F1] gives $E_N\geq-BN$, so the Boltzmann integrand is real, nonnegative and at most $e^{\beta BN}$, with a forbidden $+\infty$ configuration contributing $0$. Since $|\Lambda_L|=(2L)^d<\infty$ [F17], multiplicativity of complex modulus and its agreement with real absolute value [F21] bound the modulus of the $N$th term of $\Xi_L(z)$ by $(|z|e^{\beta B}|\Lambda_L|)^N/N!$. The sum of these bounds is finite for every $z$ by [F7], so $\Xi_L$ is entire.

Stability at $N=2$ gives $v(x)\geq-2B$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$; hence $-1\leq f_\beta(x)\leq e^{2\beta B}-1$ by [F12]. Thus for each fixed $N$ every graph term in the finite expansion $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_\beta(x_i-x_j))$ is bounded and measurable on the finite-measure box $\Lambda_L^N$. Expanding the product gives a sum over all simple graphs; each graph decomposes uniquely into connected components as in [F2]. If the component sizes are $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, assigning the $N$ labels to an ordered list of blocks contributes $N!/\prod_jm_j!$, and division by $k!$ removes block order. Integrating a product over disjoint coordinate blocks factorizes by Fubini [F5], since the factors are bounded on finite-measure boxes. Therefore the coefficient of $z^N$ in $\Xi_L$ equals that in the formal exponential of $A_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{z^n}{n!}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n$.

For $n\geq2$, integrate the pointwise tree estimate [F2] over $\Lambda_L^n$. Root each tree at vertex $1$, then remove leaves other than the root. At each removal the leaf integral over $\Lambda_L$ is at most the whole-space integral $C_\beta$ by monotonicity [F19] and translation invariance [F6]; Tonelli [F10] applies to the nonnegative tree products. The final root integral is $|\Lambda_L|$. The labelled-tree count in [F2] is $n^{n-2}$. Finite additivity [F20] sums those tree integrals, giving $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}|\Lambda_L|n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$. Thus $U_n$ is integrable on $\Lambda_L^n$. Regard its real values as complex values by the real embedding; [F21] identifies the complex modulus with real absolute value, so the integral triangle inequality [F18] gives $|b_n(L)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}/n!$. The same bound holds for $|b_n|$ by the pinned estimate [F2].

Fix $n\geq2$ and write $y_1=0$, $y_i=x_i-x_1$ for $i\geq2$. Translation invariance of $U_n$ gives $U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)$. By Tonelli [F10], translation invariance [F6], and the pinned integrability from [F2], $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n(x)|dx=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,y)|\,|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|dy\leq|\Lambda_L|\int|U_n(0,y)|dy<\infty$, using the finite cube volume [F17]. Thus the integrand is absolutely integrable and Fubini [F5] applies. Translating each remaining coordinate in its section gives $b_n(L)=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\theta_L(y)\,dy_2\cdots dy_n$, where $\theta_L(y)=\frac{|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|}{|\Lambda_L|}=\prod_{j=1}^d(1-\frac{\max_i y_{i,j}-\min_i y_{i,j}}{2L})_+$, with $r_+=\max(r,0)$. For each fixed $y$, $0\leq\theta_L(y)\leq1$ and $\theta_L(y)\to1$. The cube-intersection volume formula follows from [F17]; $U_n$ is Borel by [F11, F13, F14, F15, F16], hence measurable. For every sequence $L_m\to\infty$, dominated convergence [F4] with majorant $|U_n(0,\cdot)|$ gives $b_n(L_m)\to b_n$. If the limit as a real variable $L\to\infty$ failed, some $\epsilon>0$ would have $|b_n(L)-b_n|\geq\epsilon$ for arbitrarily large $L$; Countable Choice [A1] selects such an $L_m\geq m$ for each $m$, contradicting the sequential conclusion. Hence $b_n(L)\to b_n$.

For every integer $n\geq2$, the positive series for $e^n$ in [F7] contains the term $n^n/n!$, so $n^{n-2}/n!\leq e^n/n^2$. If $C_\beta>0$, put $q(r)=rC_\beta e^{2\beta B+1}$. For $0<r$ with $q(r)<1$, step 1.3 yields $|b_n(L)|r^n\leq r e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n^2$ and $n|b_n(L)|r^{n-1}\leq e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n$; the same bounds hold for $b_n$. Both majorant series converge. If $C_\beta=0$, step 1.3 gives $b_n(L)=b_n=0$ for $n\geq2$. Each $U_n$ is real-valued by [F2], so each coefficient $b_n(L),b_n$ is real; [F21] identifies its complex-embedding modulus with its real absolute value and gives $|z^n|=|z|^n$. Hence the coefficient and derivative majorants bound the complex power-series terms on the corresponding closed subdiscs. Thus the pressure series and their formal derivative series converge uniformly on every closed subdisc strictly inside $\mathcal D$; [F9] identifies the derivatives with the termwise derivatives.

The coefficient identity in step 1.2 is the formal identity $\Xi_L=\exp(A_L)$, and $A_L(z)=|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)$ by the definitions of $b_n(L)$. Fix a volume $L>0$ and a radius $r$ strictly inside $\mathcal D$. Step 2.1 gives $\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$, so $\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n=|\Lambda_L|\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$ for this fixed volume. Expanding the complex exponential in [F8], the sum of absolute values of all terms is bounded by $\exp(\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n)$; hence its products and coefficient sums may be regrouped, so the formal identity is an equality of convergent series and $\Xi_L(z)=\exp(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z))$. To pass to the limit on a compact subdisc $|z|\leq r$ inside $\mathcal D$, the pressure and derivative tails are uniformly bounded in $L$ by the convergent majorants of step 2.1. For each fixed $n$, step 1.4 gives coefficient convergence; finite partial sums and their derivatives therefore converge uniformly, and the uniform tail bounds give $p_L\to p$ and $p_L'\to p'$ uniformly there. [F8, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 2.1] ∎

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. All indices $n,N$ below range over $\mathbb N$. Fix $d\in\mathbb N$ with $d\geq1$, an even Borel pair potential $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with no $-\infty$ values, stable with constant $B\in\mathbb R$, $B\geq0$, and inverse parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R$ with $\beta>0$. Put $e^{-c(+\infty)}=0$ for every $c>0$, $f_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and $C_\beta=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty$. For each $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq2$, use

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j),$$

where $\mathcal C_n$ is the set of connected simple graphs on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; set $U_1=1$. For $L\in\mathbb R$ with $L>0$, let $\Lambda_L=[-L,L]^d$ and write $|\Lambda_L|:=\lambda_d(\Lambda_L)=(2L)^d$; define

$$\Xi_L(z):=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}v(x_i-x_j)\right)\,dx_1\cdots dx_N,$$

with the $N=0$ term equal to $1$. Set $b_1(L)=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n(L):=\frac1{n!|\Lambda_L|}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n.$$

Also set $b_1=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n:=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_2\cdots dx_n.$$

Let $\mathcal D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|e^{2\beta B+1}C_\beta<1\}$ when $C_\beta>0$, and let $\mathcal D=\mathbb C$ when $C_\beta=0$. On $\mathcal D$, the finite-volume connected pressure series $p_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_n(L)z^n$ and the limiting Mayer pressure series $p(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_nz^n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, are differentiable term by term, and satisfy

$$\Xi_L(z)=\exp\!\bigl(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)\bigr),\qquad \lim_{L\to\infty}p_L(z)=p(z).$$

The convergence and derivative limits are uniform on every compact subdisc of $\mathcal D$. The pressure limit here is along centered cubes only.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
